sections.content: Glycolic acid is an alpha-hydroxy acid. It loosens the bonds between dead skin cells sitting on the surface, so they come away instead of piling up.

What that looks like in practice: dullness fading, texture getting smoother, small bumps flattening, and dark patches from old spots lightening over a couple of months. What it does not do is change your skin colour, remove deep scars, or replace a dermatologist.

7% is a sensible strength. Strong enough to do something, mild enough that most people can build up to it. The 20% and 30% peels are a different product for a different purpose and should not be bought by anyone who hasn't done this one first.

sections.text: How to use it without making it worse

sections.content: Most of the complaints about this product come from using it like a normal face wash. It isn't one.

items: Start twice a week, at night, on dry clean skin. Not daily
Sweep it across with a cotton pad and leave it. Do not scrub, do not rinse it off immediately
Moisturise afterwards — glycolic acid makes dry skin drier before it makes it better
Sunblock the next morning, every time. Exfoliated skin burns faster
Stop for a week if it stings more than a light tingle, then restart once a week

sections.content: A little purging in the first two weeks is normal — small bumps surfacing as the skin turns over. Two weeks of redness and stinging is not purging, it is irritation, and the answer is to use it less.

sections.text: Original or fake: the price spread is the clue

sections.content: This is the part nobody selling it wants to explain.

The same 100ml bottle is listed across Pakistan from a few hundred rupees to around Rs. 1,999 depending on the seller. That is not normal variation for a single fixed product. Somewhere in that range, different things are being sold under the same name.
We are not going to tell you what someone else's bottle is. We can tell you what to check on any of them, including ours:

items: The label print should be sharp and straight. Crooked or blurry text is the most reliable warning sign
The bottle should have a batch number and an expiry date, printed not stickered
The liquid should be clear and thin. Cloudy or thick is wrong for a glycolic toner
Smell it. It should be faintly acidic, not perfumed like a cosmetic
Buy from a seller who will take it back. We give you 7 days and cash on delivery so you can look first

sections.text: Don't buy this toner from us if…

sections.content: You have never used an acid before and you're planning to use it every night from day one. That is how people end up with a red, tight face and a bad review they attribute to the product.
You're already using retinol, benzoyl peroxide, or another exfoliant. Stacking acids on top of each other is the fastest route to a damaged skin barrier. Pick one.
You're pregnant or breastfeeding, or you have eczema or rosacea. Ask a doctor before an AHA, not a shop.
You want to fade a dark patch in two weeks. Glycolic acid is patient. Six to eight weeks of twice-weekly use is the realistic timeline, and anyone promising faster is selling you something else.

items.q: Does Urapra glycolic acid toner work?
items.a: Yes, for texture, dullness and dark patches, if it is used twice a week at night with sunblock. It will not change your skin colour or remove deep scars.

items.q: How often should I use glycolic acid toner?
items.a: Twice a week to start, at night. Build to three or four times a week over a month or two if your skin tolerates it. Daily use from the start is the most common mistake.
Dryness, a light tingle, and two weeks of light purging are normal. Redness, stinging and flaking mean you are using it too often — cut back rather than stopping entirely.

items.q: Can I use it with retinol?
items.a: Not on the same night. Pick one. Alternating nights is safer than layering both, and starting both in the same week will tell you nothing about which one your skin objected to.
